extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and creative writers interested in Christopher Booker, narrative theory, and journalistic practice
extracted.subtask_description: Background material on Christopher Booker’s narrative theory (notably The Seven Basic Plots) and his practices/standards as a journalist and polemicist; useful for creative writers studying archetypal plot frameworks and for evaluative context on polemical/advocacy writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Seven Basic Plots (narrative archetypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker's Jungian-influenced analysis presented in The Seven Basic Plots: Why We Tell Stories — a claim that stories can be analysed and classified according to a limited set of archetypal plots and have psychological meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booker provides prescriptive generalisations about conventional plot structures. Reception notes warn that he "sets up criteria for art, and ends up condemning Rigoletto, The Cherry Orchard, Wagner, Proust, Joyce, Kafka and Lawrence … while praising Crocodile Dundee, ET and Terminator 2." Supporters describe it as an exhilarating interpretation of storytelling that gives meaning to narrative. Implication for writers: consider archetypal plot roles and psychological meanings, but be aware of critiques about over-prescription and dismissing unconventional works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prescriptiveness vs. originality in plot evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker's approach can be read as laying down evaluative criteria for 'good' stories by measuring them against conventional plot structures and psychological archetypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism (e.g., Adam Mars-Jones) highlights the anti-pattern of applying broad generalisations prescriptively to judge art; writers should note the risk of conflating typology with value and avoid excluding innovation merely because it does not fit a predefined plot category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic diligence and campaigning (qualities of strong columns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Described as the kind of journalism that 'digs, he makes the calls, he reads the small print, he takes up the cause of the little man and campaigns, he speaks truth to power without fear or favour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a model for opinion/feature writing: practice investigative thoroughness, check documentary evidence, make direct enquiries, and be willing to take up causes. Anti-pattern: lightweight aggregation and superficial blogging ('aggregation and flip bloggery'). Examples: Booker's long-running campaigning columns on family courts and social services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and responsible use of scientific evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker's articles on asbestos, passive smoking and climate change were criticised as 'misinformed' or 'substantially misleading' by scientific bodies (e.g., HSE) and commentators; reliance on contested or discredited experts was flagged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers making scientific or technical claims: verify primary literature, represent studies accurately (avoid selective quoting), check expert credentials, and anticipate institutional rebuttals; failure to do so can lead to public correction, reputational damage, and legal/ editorial consequences (example: Telegraph apology and article withdrawal over claims about Rajendra Pachauri).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polemic/sceptical framing vs balanced presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker frequently deployed sceptical/polemical framing (e.g., arguing the public is unnecessarily 'scared' about issues) and compiled criticisms of mainstream consensus, sometimes presenting those criticisms without balanced challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polemical writing can be effective as a rhetorical stance, but reviewers (e.g., Philip Ball) note the anti-pattern of presenting criticisms 'unchallenged.' Writers should balance sceptical argumentation with careful interrogation of counter-evidence and clear indication of contested points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical political writing (tone and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker co-founded Private Eye and worked as a political scriptwriter on That Was The Week That Was; his satirical work exemplifies outspoken political satire directed at named public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire as a form should aim for pointedness, informed targets, and awareness of context; examples from Booker include sketches attacking specific politicians. Satirical anti-patterns include punching without factual grounding or context that risks libel or misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaigning journalism on public policy and urbanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker campaigned against tower blocks and modernist redevelopment (Goodbye London, City of Towers) and produced campaigning documentary/journalistic work that took a clear ideological stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigning journalism often combines reportage with clear advocacy; effective practice includes documented evidence, persuasive narrative, and public engagement. Anti-patterns include ideological tunnel vision without sufficient evidence or ignoring counterarguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative as meaning-making (evaluative expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporters (e.g., Fay Weldon) frame Booker's work as interpreting storytelling as a way to give 'meaning to crude creation' — implying that strong narratives are those that provide psychological or existential meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For creative writers: consider how plot, character and structure produce meaning beyond mere events. Anti-pattern: purely gimmicky plots that lack deeper thematic or psychological resonance.
